homepage.title: Only 9% Pass This Paramedic Entrance Test
homepage.summary: Can you spot the key detail, make the clear call, and stay composed when the pressure rises?
homepage.thumbnailAlt: An ambulance ready for a paramedic-style aptitude challenge

footer.aboutText: This fictional aptitude challenge is inspired by broad professional themes such as communication, observation, teamwork, risk awareness, record keeping, inclusion, and knowing when to seek support. It does not teach clinical care and is not medical advice, emergency guidance, professional training, certification, recruitment screening, or an official paramedic assessment. Real paramedics follow current law, local protocols, employer guidance, and training appropriate to their scope of practice.

landing.quickStartText: The first calls look simple. Then every detail starts to matter.

profiles.title: You stayed composed through the toughest calls.
profiles.copy: Excellent observation, communication, and decision-making across the challenge. Your strongest area was {stage}.

profiles.title: Clear decisions as the pressure climbed.
profiles.copy: You balanced detail, teamwork, and practical judgment well. Your strongest area was {stage}.

profiles.title: A steady performance under pressure.
profiles.copy: You kept the important clues in view through several demanding calls. Your strongest area was {stage}.

profiles.title: The later calls caught you out.
profiles.copy: The hardest stages reward careful checks, clear communication, and calm priorities. Your best area was {stage}.

stageGroups.title: Scene Scan
stageGroups.encouragement: Good start. Now turn a busy scene into clear information.

questions.prompt: You arrive at a crowded building entrance. What is the smartest first move?
choices: Pause to identify hazards, access, and who needs help
questions.explanation: A quick scene scan creates a safer, clearer starting point before other decisions are made.

questions.prompt: Dispatch says ‘north entrance’; a staff member says that entrance is locked. What should happen before the team commits?
choices: Assume the staff member is right
Confirm a safe usable access point
questions.explanation: Conflicting access information should be resolved before relying on either route.

questions.prompt: A spill blocks the shortest path, while a longer corridor is clear. Which route is the sensible choice?
questions.explanation: A confirmed clear route is more useful than a shorter route with a known hazard.

questions.prompt: The scene changes and the original waiting area becomes unsafe. Which update matters first?
choices: The hazard and the new safe location
questions.explanation: The immediate change in risk and where to move are the most time-relevant facts.

questions.prompt: A crowd waves you toward a doorway, but a warning sign has fallen face-down beside it. What is the best next step?
choices: Pause at a safe point and identify what the sign says
questions.explanation: A potentially important warning should be checked before the doorway is treated as safe access.

questions.prompt: The location note says ‘loading bay’, but the first visible sign says ‘staff entrance’. What should guide your approach?
choices: Confirm the correct access point before committing
questions.explanation: A mismatch between the location note and visible signage should be resolved before committing the team.

questions.prompt: An alarm begins sounding as you approach a previously clear entrance. What has changed?
choices: The scene now needs a fresh safety check
The original plan becomes more accurate
questions.explanation: A new alarm is a meaningful change and should trigger a fresh assessment rather than automatic continuation.

stageGroups.title: First Contact
stageGroups.encouragement: Scene secure. Next, make every word count.

questions.prompt: Three people speak at once. What is the best way to regain clarity?
choices: Ask one person at a time for the key facts
questions.explanation: One speaker at a time makes important information easier to hear and confirm.

questions.prompt: Someone has difficulty hearing in the noisy room. Which response best removes the communication barrier?
choices: Move somewhere quieter and check their preferred way to communicate
Ask a bystander to decide for them
questions.explanation: Adapting the environment and checking communication preferences supports clear, respectful interaction.

questions.prompt: A person gives one location, then a different one. What is the strongest response?
questions.explanation: Conflicting information should be clarified without blame or assumption.

questions.prompt: Which opening is most likely to produce useful information?
questions.explanation: A clear, neutral prompt invites specific information without leading the answer.

questions.prompt: A person understands only part of your question. What is the clearest response?
choices: Use plain words, one idea at a time, and check understanding
questions.explanation: Plain language and a simple check-back reduce misunderstanding without making assumptions.

questions.prompt: Someone is upset and needs extra time to answer. What is most likely to help?
choices: Allow a pause, then ask one clear question
questions.explanation: A calm pause and one focused question can make it easier for useful information to emerge.

questions.prompt: You hear a surname two different ways. What is the safest communication check?
choices: Ask the person to confirm it and repeat it back
questions.explanation: Confirming and repeating back a key detail is clearer than guessing.

stageGroups.title: Sharp Observation
stageGroups.encouragement: You noticed the change. Now separate facts from assumptions.

questions.prompt: Which note is the most objective?
choices: The person was seated and answering questions at 14:10
questions.explanation: It records observable facts and a time rather than an interpretation.

questions.prompt: At 09:05 the east door is open. At 09:12 it is locked. What is the key observation?
questions.explanation: The operationally relevant change is that a previously open access point is now locked.

questions.prompt: Board A: P2 · 16:20 · NORTHBAY. Board B: P5 · 16:20 · NORTHBAY. Which detail differs?
questions.explanation: The time and destination match; only the platform changes.

questions.prompt: A direct witness describes what they saw. Another person repeats something heard third-hand. Which account should be checked first?
questions.explanation: A direct account is a stronger starting point, while still requiring appropriate checking.

questions.prompt: Log 1 reads ‘14:32 · Gate C · open’. Log 2 reads ‘14:32 · Gate G · open’. What changed?
questions.explanation: The time and access status match; the gate letter is the only changed detail.

questions.prompt: Which statement separates observation from assumption?
choices: The bag was left beside the chair at 11:05
questions.explanation: It records something visible and time-specific without assigning motive or judgment.

questions.prompt: A note says ‘vehicle moved after the update’ but gives no time. Which missing detail would make the sequence clearest?
questions.explanation: A time marker allows the movement to be placed accurately in the sequence of events.

stageGroups.title: Clear Comms
stageGroups.encouragement: Message received. Now keep the whole team aligned.

questions.prompt: A useful update must include location, issue, and access. Which message includes all three?
choices: Third floor, elevator unavailable, use west stairs
questions.explanation: It supplies the location, the access issue, and a usable route.

questions.prompt: A radio message breaks up: ‘...east... closed... use...’ What should the receiver do?
choices: Request and confirm the key details
questions.explanation: A broken message should be clarified before it guides action.

questions.prompt: Which phrase is least useful in a location update?
questions.explanation: ‘Over there’ has no stable reference point and can easily be misunderstood.

questions.prompt: A route change requires team-lead confirmation. The lead confirms it. What can the crew do next?
questions.explanation: Once the stated confirmation requirement is met, the team can use the updated route.

questions.prompt: You receive the instruction ‘Use south access, not east.’ Which reply best closes the loop?
choices: I heard something about a door
questions.explanation: Repeating the key instruction confirms that the critical detail was heard correctly.

questions.prompt: Which update is easiest for another team to act on?
choices: Arrival in approximately six minutes at the west entrance
questions.explanation: It provides a usable time estimate and a specific meeting point.

questions.prompt: Two team members interpret a hand signal differently. What should happen next?
choices: Pause and confirm the intended instruction verbally
questions.explanation: When a signal is ambiguous, a direct confirmation restores a shared understanding.

stageGroups.title: Route Logic
stageGroups.encouragement: Route set. Next, organize people as carefully as information.

questions.prompt: Route A takes 8 minutes but its gate may be locked. Route B takes 11 minutes and is confirmed open. Which is the reliable choice right now?
questions.explanation: Route B is confirmed usable; Route A's shorter time depends on uncertain access.

questions.prompt: You leave at 13:25. Travel takes 18 minutes and access takes 4 more. When are you ready to enter?
questions.explanation: Eighteen minutes gives 13:43, then four more gives 13:47.

questions.prompt: The west road adds 6 minutes. The original 12-minute journey now takes how long?
questions.explanation: Twelve minutes plus a six-minute diversion equals 18 minutes.

questions.prompt: Two routes both take 15 minutes. One has a known closure; the other is clear. What breaks the tie?
questions.explanation: With equal journey times, the confirmed clear route is the dependable option.

questions.prompt: Travel takes 14 minutes, parking takes 3, and the walk to the entrance takes 5. What is the total access time?
questions.explanation: Fourteen plus three plus five gives a total of 22 minutes.

questions.prompt: You must visit Checkpoint B before Checkpoint D. Which sequence follows the rule?
questions.explanation: Only the B-to-D sequence respects the stated order.

questions.prompt: Route A takes 10 minutes plus an 8-minute delay. Route B takes 16 minutes with no delay. Which is quicker now?
questions.explanation: Route A totals 18 minutes, so the 16-minute Route B is two minutes quicker.

stageGroups.title: Teamwork
stageGroups.encouragement: Team aligned. Now handle the professional judgment calls.

questions.prompt: One team member checks access while another keeps the only working radio. What must be agreed first?
questions.explanation: Split roles work safely only when the team knows how and when to reconnect.

questions.prompt: Two tasks are waiting. One affects immediate scene safety; the other is a routine stock note. Which leads?
questions.explanation: The live safety issue has the higher immediate priority.

questions.prompt: A colleague spots that the address has changed. What is the strongest team response?
choices: Let each person choose an address
Confirm the change and update the shared plan
questions.explanation: Confirming and sharing the change keeps the team working from the same information.

questions.prompt: One available crew has the right equipment but is farther away. Another is closer but lacks it. What matters before assignment?
questions.explanation: Resource decisions should match the capabilities required for the specific task.

questions.prompt: Three tasks need owners. What is the strongest way to divide them?
choices: Match each task to capability, confirm ownership, and set a check-in
Give every task to the fastest person
questions.explanation: Clear ownership matched to capability reduces duplication and missed work.

questions.prompt: Two colleagues disagree about the next route. What is the most constructive response?
choices: Compare the current facts and escalate if the conflict remains
Take separate routes without telling anyone
questions.explanation: A fact-based check keeps disagreement useful and provides a route to resolution.

questions.prompt: A teammate says they missed the latest update. What best restores the shared plan?
choices: Repeat every event from the day
Give a brief update and ask them to confirm their role
questions.explanation: A concise recap plus role confirmation gets the whole team aligned again.

stageGroups.title: Respect & Scope
stageGroups.encouragement: Professional instincts strong. The next stage adds time pressure.

questions.prompt: Someone asks you to perform a task outside your training. What is the most professional response?
choices: Recognize the limit and seek appropriate support
Ask a bystander to do it
questions.explanation: Knowing the limits of your role and seeking support protects everyone involved.

questions.prompt: A person prefers to receive information slowly and in short steps. What should you do?
choices: Adapt the explanation and check understanding
questions.explanation: Communication should be adapted to the person's needs and understanding checked.

questions.prompt: A nearby resident asks for private details about the call. What is the appropriate default?
questions.explanation: Private information should not be shared merely because someone is curious.

questions.prompt: A person wants to be involved in decisions about what happens next. What is the respectful approach?
choices: Give relevant information and support their involvement
questions.explanation: People should be supported to take an appropriate role in decisions that concern them.

questions.prompt: A person asks for a support person to be present during an explanation. What is the best starting point?
choices: Consider the request, privacy, and the person's preferences
Ask the support person to make every decision
questions.explanation: The person's preferences and privacy should shape how support is included.

questions.prompt: A communication preference is unfamiliar to you. What is the most respectful response?
choices: Ask what would help and seek appropriate support if needed
questions.explanation: Asking rather than assuming helps make communication accessible and respectful.

questions.prompt: You notice an error in a record you are allowed to update. What is the professional approach?
choices: Delete the whole record without explanation
Follow the proper correction process so the record remains clear
Leave the error for someone else
questions.explanation: A transparent correction preserves the accuracy and integrity of the record.

stageGroups.title: Under Pressure
stageGroups.encouragement: You kept your head. Now make the handover bulletproof.

questions.prompt: Thirty seconds remain. Update A is confirmed; Update B is newer but its source is unreadable. What comes first?
questions.explanation: Time pressure does not turn uncertain information into reliable information.

questions.prompt: A familiar shortcut is reported blocked today. A longer route is confirmed open. Which fact deserves more weight?
questions.explanation: Current verified conditions are more relevant than familiarity.

questions.prompt: A caller changes the apartment from 18 to 81. What should happen before arrival?
questions.explanation: A transposed location detail can redirect the whole response and should be confirmed.

questions.prompt: The team is overloaded with information. What is the best way to reduce error?
choices: Prioritize, summarize, and confirm the key actions
questions.explanation: A short prioritized summary helps the team maintain a shared, accurate plan.

questions.prompt: A countdown is running, but the destination code is missing one digit. What is the best response?
choices: Confirm the code before it directs the team
questions.explanation: Urgency makes accurate confirmation more important, not less.

questions.prompt: Two updates arrive together: one reports a new access hazard; the other changes a routine meeting time. Which should be handled first?
questions.explanation: A new safety-relevant change takes priority over a routine scheduling update.

questions.prompt: An interruption makes you lose your place during a critical summary. What is the safest recovery?
choices: Pause, return to the last confirmed point, and restate the key actions
questions.explanation: Returning to the last confirmed point prevents an interruption from creating a hidden gap.

stageGroups.title: Handover & Reset
stageGroups.encouragement: Clean handover. One final shift stands between you and the result.

questions.prompt: Which handover is clearest?
choices: Adult seated, alert, speaking clearly; change noted at 09:20
questions.explanation: It gives observable facts and a useful time marker.

questions.prompt: Why use a checklist before leaving?
choices: It reduces the chance of missing an important item
It removes the need to communicate
questions.explanation: A checklist is a backstop against avoidable omissions, not a replacement for professional decisions.

questions.prompt: A kit seal is unexpectedly broken before use. What is the sensible first action?
choices: Report it and follow the appropriate equipment check
questions.explanation: Unexpected equipment status should be reported and checked under the relevant procedure.

questions.prompt: Which record entry is most useful?
choices: Access changed from east to west at 17:42; control updated
questions.explanation: It records the specific change, time, and communication action.

questions.prompt: A handover is complete, but the receiving colleague has not confirmed the new access route. What remains to be done?
choices: Ask for confirmation of the route
Remove the route from the record
questions.explanation: Confirmation closes the communication loop on a detail that could redirect the next team.

questions.prompt: After a call, one frequently used item is missing from its usual place. What is the best reset action?
choices: Record, report, and resolve the missing item through the normal process
Replace it with an unrelated item
questions.explanation: A clear equipment reset helps the next response begin ready and avoids passing on a hidden problem.

questions.prompt: Which handover sequence is easiest to follow?
choices: Current situation → key changes → actions completed → what is still needed
questions.explanation: A structured sequence lets the receiving person understand the present state and remaining actions quickly.

questions.prompt: Final call: east entrance is locked, west entrance is open, and control still lists east. What is the best complete action?
choices: Confirm west, update control, and brief the team
Wait for the board to change itself
questions.explanation: The action verifies current access and keeps both control and the team aligned.

questions.prompt: A direct witness says Gate B. A second-hand message says Gate D. The board is blank. What should guide the next step?
choices: Choose D because it is later in the alphabet
Verify the direct account and access
questions.explanation: The direct account is the stronger starting point, but access still needs confirmation.

questions.prompt: Route A takes 12 minutes but has unconfirmed access. Route B takes 16 minutes and is confirmed clear. If reliability comes first, which route wins?
questions.explanation: Under the stated rule, confirmed Route B outranks the faster uncertain option.

questions.prompt: The scene is safe, the location is confirmed, roles are assigned, and the radio check is complete. What is the strongest next move?
choices: Proceed with the shared plan and keep monitoring for change
questions.explanation: With the key checks complete, the team can act while remaining alert to new information.

questions.prompt: Control gives Gate A. A time-stamped site update says Gate A closed two minutes ago and Gate C is open. What is the best complete response?
choices: Confirm the site update, advise control, and brief the team on Gate C
questions.explanation: The response verifies the newer operational detail and keeps everyone working from the same plan.

questions.prompt: Route North takes 9 minutes plus 7 minutes for access. Route South takes 13 minutes plus 1 minute for access. Which reaches the entry point first?
questions.explanation: North totals 16 minutes and South totals 14, so South reaches the entry point two minutes sooner.

questions.prompt: One final update is uncertain, the scene is stable, and the team is ready. What best balances speed and reliability?
choices: Act on the uncertain detail without telling anyone
Confirm the detail that could change the plan, then proceed with a shared update
questions.explanation: The key uncertainty should be resolved without discarding the reliable work already completed.
